claim: Myxococcus xanthus is a soil-dwelling δ-proteobacterium that exhibits a complex multicellular life cycle with two phases: growth and starvation-induced development.
source: Myxococcus xanthus is a soil-dwelling δ-proteobacterium that exhibits a complex multicellular life cycle with two phases: growth and starvation-induced development (Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016.

claim: When nutrients are available, M. xanthus cells divide to produce a community known as swarm.
source: When nutrients are available, cells divide to produce a community known as swarm.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the growth phase behavior.

claim: M. xanthus swarms are predatory (although not obligate) and can digest prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms.
source: Swarms are predatory (although not obligate) and can digest prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms (Pérez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pérez et al., 2016.

claim: Upon starvation, M. xanthus cells enter a developmental program during which they migrate into aggregation centers and climb on top of each other to build macroscopic structures termed fruiting bodies.
source: Upon starvation, cells in the swarm enter a developmental program, during which they migrate into aggregation centers and climb on top of each other to build macroscopic structures termed fruiting bodies.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the developmental response to starvation.

claim: To form fruiting bodies, starving M. xanthus cells glide on solid surfaces using two motility systems: A- (adventurous) and S- (social) motility.
source: To form fruiting bodies, starving cells glide on solid surfaces by using two motility systems, known as A- (adventurous) and S- (social) motility, which allow individual cell movement or group movement that requires cell-cell contact, respectively (Mauriello et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2014; Islam and Mignot, 2015; Chang et al., 2016; Schumacher and Søgaard-Andersen, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A-motility allows individual cell movement in M. xanthus.
source: To form fruiting bodies, starving cells glide on solid surfaces by using two motility systems, known as A- (adventurous) and S- (social) motility, which allow individual cell movement or group movement that requires cell-cell contact, respectively (Mauriello et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2014; Islam and Mignot, 2015; Chang et al., 2016; Schumacher and Søgaard-Andersen, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the function of A-motility.

claim: S-motility allows group movement that requires cell-cell contact in M. xanthus.
source: To form fruiting bodies, starving cells glide on solid surfaces by using two motility systems, known as A- (adventurous) and S- (social) motility, which allow individual cell movement or group movement that requires cell-cell contact, respectively (Mauriello et al., 2010; Nan et al., 2014; Islam and Mignot, 2015; Chang et al., 2016; Schumacher and Søgaard-Andersen, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the function of S-motility.

claim: After completion of aggregation (24 hr post-starvation), M. xanthus cells differentiate into environmentally resistant myxospores.
source: After completion of aggregation (24 hr post-starvation), cells differentiate into environmentally resistant myxospores, which are embedded in a complex extracellular matrix (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: Each M. xanthus fruiting body contains approximately 10^5–10^6 myxospores.
source: Each fruiting body contains ≈105–106 myxospores.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about fruiting body composition.

claim: Only approximately 10% of the starving M. xanthus population become myxospores.
source: Interestingly, only ≈10% of the starving population become myxospores (O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a) as most cells (around 60%) undergo programmed cell death, most likely to provide the rest of the population enough nutrients to successfully build fruiting bodies (Wireman and Dworkin, 1977; Nariya and Inouye, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a.

claim: Around 60% of starving M. xanthus cells undergo programmed cell death.
source: Interestingly, only ≈10% of the starving population become myxospores (O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a) as most cells (around 60%) undergo programmed cell death, most likely to provide the rest of the population enough nutrients to successfully build fruiting bodies (Wireman and Dworkin, 1977; Nariya and Inouye, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wireman and Dworkin, 1977 and Nariya and Inouye, 2008.

claim: Programmed cell death in M. xanthus development likely provides nutrients to the rest of the population to successfully build fruiting bodies.
source: Interestingly, only ≈10% of the starving population become myxospores (O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a) as most cells (around 60%) undergo programmed cell death, most likely to provide the rest of the population enough nutrients to successfully build fruiting bodies (Wireman and Dworkin, 1977; Nariya and Inouye, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and uses speculative language ('most likely').

claim: The remaining M. xanthus cells differentiate into a persister-like state termed peripheral rods (PR), which surround the fruiting bodies.
source: The remaining cells differentiate into a persister-like state, termed peripheral rods (PR), which surround the fruiting bodies (O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a; O'Connor and Zusman, 1991b; O'Connor and Zusman, 1991c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to O'Connor and Zusman, 1991a, 1991b, and 1991c.

claim: Peripheral rods are morphologically similar to vegetative M. xanthus cells.
source: While PRs are morphologically similar to vegetative cells, myxospores are coccoid and are surrounded by a thick coat mainly consisting of polysaccharides (Kottel et al., 1975; Müller et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2012; Holkenbrink et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct comparative statement about PR morphology.

claim: M. xanthus myxospores are coccoid and are surrounded by a thick coat mainly consisting of polysaccharides.
source: While PRs are morphologically similar to vegetative cells, myxospores are coccoid and are surrounded by a thick coat mainly consisting of polysaccharides (Kottel et al., 1975; Müller et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2012; Holkenbrink et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing myxospore structure.

claim: M. xanthus myxospores can germinate when nutrients are available.
source: Myxospores can germinate when nutrients are available, and collective germination of myxospores from a fruiting body generates a small swarm that facilitates cooperative feeding.
evidence: This is a direct statement about myxospore germination conditions.

claim: Collective germination of myxospores from a fruiting body generates a small swarm that facilitates cooperative feeding.
source: Myxospores can germinate when nutrients are available, and collective germination of myxospores from a fruiting body generates a small swarm that facilitates cooperative feeding.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the outcome of collective germination.

claim: The M. xanthus developmental program is directed by sophisticated genetic regulatory networks coupled to intra- and extra-cellular cues.
source: The developmental program is directed by sophisticated, but not completely defined, genetic regulatory networks, which are coupled to a series of intra- and extra-cellular cues (Kroos, 2017; Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kroos, 2017 and Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016.

claim: Starvation triggers accumulation of cyclic-di-GMP in M. xanthus cells.
source: The first cue is starvation, which triggers accumulation of cyclic-di-GMP and, via the stringent response, guanosine penta- and tetraphosphate [(p)ppGpp] inside the cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the molecular response to starvation.

claim: Starvation triggers accumulation of guanosine penta- and tetraphosphate [(p)ppGpp] via the stringent response in M. xanthus cells.
source: The first cue is starvation, which triggers accumulation of cyclic-di-GMP and, via the stringent response, guanosine penta- and tetraphosphate [(p)ppGpp] inside the cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stringent response to starvation.

claim: Four master cascade modules (Nla24, Mrp, FruA, and bacterial enhancer-binding proteins [bEBPs]) control the timing of gene expression during M. xanthus development.
source: These global signals somehow activate four master cascade modules (Nla24, Mrp, FruA, and bacterial enhancer-binding proteins [bEBPs]), which interconnect to control the correct timing of gene expression (Kroos, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kroos, 2017.

claim: Proper progression of M. xanthus development requires intercellular communication via five sequential extracellular signals named A, B, C, D, and E.
source: Proper progression of development requires intercellular communication, wherein cells produce and transmit five sequential extracellular signals, named A, B, C, D, and E (Bretl and Kirby, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bretl and Kirby, 2016.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis revealed that 1415 genes (19.6% of M. xanthus genes) had statistically significant changes in transcript abundance during development.
source: We found that at least 19.6% of M. xanthus genes (1415/7229) had statistically significant changes in transcript abundance during development.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNA-Seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: Global gene expression patterns were examined by RNA-Seq analysis of M. xanthus strain DK1622 developed on nutrient limited CF agar plates.
source: Global gene expression patterns were examined by RNA-Seq analysis of the wild-type M. xanthus strain DK1622 developed on nutrient limited CF agar plates.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: RNA was harvested from two independent biological replicates at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 hr of M. xanthus development.
source: RNA was harvested from two independent biological replicates at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 hr of development, reverse transcribed to cDNA, and sequenced by Illumina methodology.
evidence: This describes the experimental sampling strategy.

claim: On average, 54.72 million read pairs and a coverage of 591X was obtained from the RNA-Seq analysis.
source: On average, 54.72 million read pairs and a coverage of 591X was obtained.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing analysis.

claim: After removing ribosomal sequences, the genome coverage varied from 5.52 to 14.18X with a median of 10.49X.
source: After removing the ribosomal sequences, the genome coverage varied from 5.52 to 14.18X (median of 10.49X), enough to provide an adequate coverage of the mRNA fraction.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data processing.

claim: The two sample-replicates showed a high degree of concordance in gene expression (R2 correlation >0.98), with the exception of 24 hr samples (R2 correlation = 0.80).
source: The two sample-replicates showed a high degree of concordance in gene expression (R2 correlation >0.98), with the exception of 24 hr samples (R2correlation = 0.80), which may be related to lack of synchrony between cells in the transition from aggregation to sporulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the replicate comparison analysis.

claim: The lower correlation at 24 hr may be related to lack of synchrony between cells in the transition from aggregation to sporulation.
source: The two sample-replicates showed a high degree of concordance in gene expression (R2 correlation >0.98), with the exception of 24 hr samples (R2correlation = 0.80), which may be related to lack of synchrony between cells in the transition from aggregation to sporulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lower correlation at 24 hr.

claim: Developmentally regulated genes were organized into 10 developmental groups (DGs) based on expression patterns.
source: 1415 significantly regulated genes (90.9% of the genes passing quality control) were then analyzed for clusters of similar expression patterns. Briefly, initial evaluation of several clustering methods (see Materials and methods for details) revealed kmeans clustering with 6–12 clusters produced the best clustering of genes with similar expression profiles. Refinement of kmeans clusters by visual inspection indicated 10 DGs best explained the number of unique gene profiles (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis and is supported by Figure 3A.

claim: DGs 1 and 2 contained genes that were immediately down-regulated relative to growth conditions.
source: DGs 1 and 2 contained genes that were immediately down-regulated relative to growth conditions, DGs 3–5 correlated with the aggregation phase, DGs 6–7 correlated with the transition from aggregation to sporulation, and DGs 8–10 correlated with the sporulation phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of DGs 1 and 2 as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DGs 3–5 correlated with the aggregation phase of M. xanthus development.
source: DGs 1 and 2 contained genes that were immediately down-regulated relative to growth conditions, DGs 3–5 correlated with the aggregation phase, DGs 6–7 correlated with the transition from aggregation to sporulation, and DGs 8–10 correlated with the sporulation phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of DGs 3-5 as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DGs 6–7 correlated with the transition from aggregation to sporulation in M. xanthus development.
source: DGs 1 and 2 contained genes that were immediately down-regulated relative to growth conditions, DGs 3–5 correlated with the aggregation phase, DGs 6–7 correlated with the transition from aggregation to sporulation, and DGs 8–10 correlated with the sporulation phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of DGs 6-7 as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DGs 8–10 correlated with the sporulation phase of M. xanthus development.
source: DGs 1 and 2 contained genes that were immediately down-regulated relative to growth conditions, DGs 3–5 correlated with the aggregation phase, DGs 6–7 correlated with the transition from aggregation to sporulation, and DGs 8–10 correlated with the sporulation phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of DGs 8-10 as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The number of genes in each developmental cluster ranged from 5.5% (DG3) to 14.1% (DG8).
source: The number of genes attributed to each cluster ranged from 5.5% (DG3) to 14.1% (DG8) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 21.8% of developmentally regulated genes exhibited peak expressions during growth.
source: Similar proportions of genes exhibited peak expressions in growth (21.8%), aggregation (23.8%), and transition from aggregation to sporulation (18.8%) phases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression pattern analysis.

claim: 23.8% of developmentally regulated genes exhibited peak expressions during aggregation.
source: Similar proportions of genes exhibited peak expressions in growth (21.8%), aggregation (23.8%), and transition from aggregation to sporulation (18.8%) phases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression pattern analysis.

claim: 18.8% of developmentally regulated genes exhibited peak expressions during the transition from aggregation to sporulation.
source: Similar proportions of genes exhibited peak expressions in growth (21.8%), aggregation (23.8%), and transition from aggregation to sporulation (18.8%) phases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression pattern analysis.

claim: 35.6% of developmentally regulated genes exhibited peak expressions during the sporulation phase.
source: The final phase accounted for peak expressions of 35.6% of genes, consistent with the significant morphological and physiological rewiring that must occur during spore differentiation and preparation for extended quiescence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression pattern analysis with an interpretation.

claim: The high proportion of genes with peak expression during sporulation is consistent with significant morphological and physiological rewiring during spore differentiation.
source: The final phase accounted for peak expressions of 35.6% of genes, consistent with the significant morphological and physiological rewiring that must occur during spore differentiation and preparation for extended quiescence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on biological knowledge.

claim: The number of genes accounting for 50% of all mRNA expression was low (~300) during growth and steadily increased to 762 by the end of sporulation.
source: When the number of genes by RPKM values that account for 50% of all mRNA expression at each time point was compared, it was observed that this number was low (~300) during growth, and at 48 hr it steadily increases to 762 by the end of sporulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The transcriptome becomes distributed across a broader number of genes during M. xanthus development.
source: This suggests that the transcriptome is becoming distributed across a broader number of genes during development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on gene expression distribution.

claim: Of approximately 280 characterized M. xanthus developmental genes, 167 were included in the developmental groups.
source: As a first step in analysis of the DGs, genes that have been previously described to affect M. xanthus development were identified. Of the ~280 characterized genes, 167 were included in the DGs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing known genes to the DGs.

claim: Most characterized developmental genes showed peak expression patterns at a time point that matched with the developmental phase where they have been reported to function.
source: Most showed peak expression patterns at a time point that matched with the developmental phase where they have been reported to function, some of which have a well-defined role on development (Figure 3—source data 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from comparing expression patterns to known functions.

claim: 92% (218/237) of genes significantly up-regulated in the sporulation transcriptome were also significantly up-regulated in the developmental transcriptome.
source: 92% (218/237) of genes significantly up-regulated (>2 fold) in the sporulation transcriptome were also significantly up-regulated in the developmental transcriptome.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparing the two transcriptome datasets.

claim: Genes up-regulated in the sporulation transcriptome were significantly over-represented in DGs 7 and 8.
source: These genes were significantly over-represented in DGs 7 and 8, with low probability (p) that this association is due to random chance (p=1×10−12 and p=2×10−11, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of transcriptome datasets.

claim: A-motility genes were up-regulated during early M. xanthus development.
source: A-motility genes were up-regulated during early development, while S-motility genes first decreased at 6 hr, and then returned to growth levels during aggregation (except for pilA), suggesting that A motility is preferentially used by cells during aggregation.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis of motility genes.

claim: S-motility genes first decreased at 6 hr, and then returned to growth levels during aggregation (except for pilA).
source: A-motility genes were up-regulated during early development, while S-motility genes first decreased at 6 hr, and then returned to growth levels during aggregation (except for pilA), suggesting that A motility is preferentially used by cells during aggregation.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis of motility genes.

claim: A motility is preferentially used by M. xanthus cells during aggregation.
source: A-motility genes were up-regulated during early development, while S-motility genes first decreased at 6 hr, and then returned to growth levels during aggregation (except for pilA), suggesting that A motility is preferentially used by cells during aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns of A- and S-motility genes.

claim: During sporulation, expression of genes encoding both A- and S-motility engines decreased.
source: During sporulation, expression of genes encoding both motility engines decreased (Figure 4), although some of them peaked again at this stage.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The peak of some A-motility genes during sporulation is consistent with the repurposing of certain A-motility proteins to function in spore coat assembly.
source: The peak of some A-motility genes during sporulation is consistent with the repurposing of certain A-motility proteins to function in spore coat assembly (Wartel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to Wartel et al., 2013.

claim: M. xanthus does not appear to consume sugars as carbon or energy sources during growth.
source: During growth, M. xanthus does not appear to consume sugars as carbon or energy sources (Watson and Dworkin, 1968; Bretscher and Kaiser, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Watson and Dworkin, 1968 and Bretscher and Kaiser, 1978.

claim: During growth, M. xanthus efficiently utilizes pyruvate, amino acids, and lipids which directly enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.
source: Instead, pyruvate, amino acids, and lipids are efficiently utilized which directly enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (Bretscher and Kaiser, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bretscher and Kaiser, 1978.

claim: Most genes involved in energy generation (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) were found in DG2.
source: Analysis of the DGs revealed that most genes involved in energy generation (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) were found in DG2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Energy generation genes are down-regulated at 6 hr but later up-regulated at lower levels than during growth.
source: Therefore, although they are down-regulated at 6 hr, they are later up-regulated at lower levels than during growth.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of energy generation genes.

claim: Many genes encoding enzymes of the glycolytic/gluconeogenic pathway were up-regulated during M. xanthus development, with most reaching maximum expression levels at the completion of aggregation (24–48 hr).
source: In contrast, many genes encoding enzymes of the glycolytic/gluconeogenic pathway were up-regulated during development, with most reaching maximum expression levels at the completion of aggregation (24–48 hr) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Developmental up-regulation of the glycolytic pathway genes may allow developing cells to obtain energy from sugars released from cells undergoing developmental lysis or from glycogen.
source: For instance, developmental up-regulation of the glycolytic pathway genes may allow developing cells to obtain energy from sugars released from cells undergoing developmental lysis or from glycogen.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the glycolytic gene expression pattern.

claim: Glycogen accumulates during late stationary phase/early development in M. xanthus, and then disappears prior to sporulation.
source: Glycogen accumulates during late stationary phase/early development, and then disappears prior to sporulation (Nariya and Inouye, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nariya and Inouye, 2003.

claim: Enzymes predicted to be involved in synthesis of glycogen, such as GlgC, were found in DG4.
source: Enzymes predicted to be involved in synthesis of glycogen, such as GlgC, were found in DG4, while enzymes involved in utilization of glycogen, such as trehalose synthase, GlgP, and MalQ appeared to be constitutively expressed.
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis.

claim: Enzymes involved in utilization of glycogen, such as trehalose synthase, GlgP, and MalQ appeared to be constitutively expressed.
source: Enzymes predicted to be involved in synthesis of glycogen, such as GlgC, were found in DG4, while enzymes involved in utilization of glycogen, such as trehalose synthase, GlgP, and MalQ appeared to be constitutively expressed.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis.

claim: Regulation of glycogen production/consumption is likely regulated post-transcriptionally, as has been demonstrated by phosphorylation of PfkA by Pkn4.
source: The observation that these competing pathways show overlapping expression profiles suggests that regulation of glycogen production/consumption is likely regulated post-transcriptionally, as has been demonstrated by phosphorylation of PfkA by Pkn4 (Nariya and Inouye, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on expression patterns and supported by a citation.

claim: Lipid bodies accumulate in M. xanthus cells prior to sporulation.
source: Lipid bodies also accumulate in cells prior to sporulation. They mainly consist of triacylglycerides derived from membrane phospholipids as cells shorten in length, which are later used as an energy source (Hoiczyk et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoiczyk et al., 2009 and Bhat et al., 2014.

claim: Lipid bodies mainly consist of triacylglycerides derived from membrane phospholipids as cells shorten in length.
source: Lipid bodies also accumulate in cells prior to sporulation. They mainly consist of triacylglycerides derived from membrane phospholipids as cells shorten in length, which are later used as an energy source (Hoiczyk et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoiczyk et al., 2009 and Bhat et al., 2014.

claim: Lipid bodies are later used as an energy source during M. xanthus development.
source: Lipid bodies also accumulate in cells prior to sporulation. They mainly consist of triacylglycerides derived from membrane phospholipids as cells shorten in length, which are later used as an energy source (Hoiczyk et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoiczyk et al., 2009 and Bhat et al., 2014.

claim: Genes involved in lipid degradation reached maximum expression at 24–48 hr (β-oxidation) or even at later times (by other pathways).
source: On the other hand, genes involved in lipid degradation reached maximum expression at 24–48 hr (β-oxidation) or even at later times (by other pathways) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Lipids are preferably consumed during sporulation in M. xanthus.
source: These fatty acid degradation enzyme profiles suggest that lipids are preferably consumed during sporulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of lipid degradation genes.

claim: Four glycosyl hydrolases were specifically up-regulated during M. xanthus development.
source: Moreover, the observation that four glycosyl hydrolases were specifically up-regulated during development (Figure 7A) suggests the cells may recycle vegetative polysaccharides or scavenge polysaccharides released from cells induced to lyse.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: M. xanthus cells may recycle vegetative polysaccharides or scavenge polysaccharides released from cells induced to lyse during development.
source: Moreover, the observation that four glycosyl hydrolases were specifically up-regulated during development (Figure 7A) suggests the cells may recycle vegetative polysaccharides or scavenge polysaccharides released from cells induced to lyse.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the expression of glycosyl hydrolases.

claim: 60 proteases appeared in the 10 developmental groups.
source: Consistently, 60 proteases appeared in the 10 DGs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DG analysis.

claim: 16 proteases were specific to growth and down-regulated after 6 hr of starvation.
source: 16 of these were specific to growth and down-regulated after 6 hr of starvation, while the rest were sequentially up-regulated at different time points (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: M. xanthus produces multiple secondary metabolites, some of which (i.e. myxovirescine and myxoprincomide) facilitate predation.
source: M. xanthus produces multiple SMs, some of which (i.e. myxovirescine and myxoprincomide) facilitate predation (Xiao et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2011 and Müller et al., 2016.

claim: Genes responsible for myxovirescine and myxoprincomide biosynthesis are expressed during growth, but their expression increases during development.
source: However, we have found that although genes responsible for their biosynthesis are expressed during growth, their expression increases during development (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: The M. xanthus genome codes for 18 nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS), 22 polyketide synthases (PKS), and six mixed PKS/NRPS genes located in regions predicted to be involved in secondary metabolite synthesis.
source: The M. xanthus genome codes for 18 nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS), 22 polyketide synthases (PKS), and six mixed PKS/NRPS genes located in regions predicted to be involved in SMs synthesis (Korp et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Korp et al., 2016.

claim: 10 NRPS/PKS/mixed PKS-NRPS genes were developmentally up-regulated, and 9/10 were found in DGs 8, 9 and 10.
source: Of these, 10 were developmentally up-regulated, and 9/10 were found in DGs 8, 9 and 10 (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: 129 genes assigned to the DGs were located in secondary metabolite regions.
source: Moreover, 129 genes assigned to the DGs were located in those SM regions (Korp et al., 2016), and 51 of these were also identified in DGs 8, 9, and 10 (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from comparing DG genes to secondary metabolite regions.

claim: 51 genes in secondary metabolite regions were identified in DGs 8, 9, and 10.
source: Moreover, 129 genes assigned to the DGs were located in those SM regions (Korp et al., 2016), and 51 of these were also identified in DGs 8, 9, and 10 (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis.

claim: Secondary metabolites may play previously unrecognized roles during M. xanthus development.
source: Together, these observations suggest that SMs may play previously unrecognized roles during development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the expression patterns of secondary metabolite genes.

claim: The protein composition of ribosome complexes purified from growing M. xanthus cells versus myxospores was different.
source: It was previously reported that the protein composition of ribosome complexes purified from growing cells versus myxospores was different (Foster and Parish, 1973), but this intriguing observation has not been further pursued.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foster and Parish, 1973.

claim: 76 genes involved in translation fit the criteria for inclusion in the developmental groups, representing 5.4% of the genes included in them.
source: 76 genes involved in translation fit the criteria for inclusion in the DGs, which represents 5.4% of the genes included in them.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DG analysis.

claim: Most genes involved in translation are down-regulated by 6 hr, likely as the result of the stringent response.
source: Most of the genes involved in translation (i.e. encoding ribosomal proteins, initiation, elongation and termination factors, ribosome maturation and modification proteins, and several aminoacyl-tRNA ligases) are down-regulated by 6 hr, likely as the result of the stringent response (Starosta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis with an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Most translation genes were subsequently up-regulated to a level similar to, or even higher than that observed during growth.
source: Interestingly, most of them were subsequently up-regulated to a level similar to, or even higher than that observed during growth (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: M. xanthus encodes two paralogs for ribosomal proteins S1, S4, S14, L28, and L33.
source: M. xanthus encodes two paralogs for proteins S1, S4, S14, L28, and L33 (Table 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from genome analysis.

claim: The two S4 paralogs exhibit similar RPKM values during growth, but the RPKM for MXAN_RS16120 was 10-fold higher than that for MXAN_RS32955 at 48 hr of development.
source: Most notably, the two S4 paralogs were in the DGs, and exhibit similar RPKM values during growth. However, the RPKM for MXAN_RS16120 was 10-fold higher than that for MXAN_RS32955 at 48 hr of development (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Regulation of translational machinery may play an important role in directing the M. xanthus developmental program.
source: While it is possible that some of the transcriptional changes observed in the translational machinery could be related to ribosomal hibernation in myxospores and/or PRs (Yoshida and Wada, 2014; Harms et al., 2016; Gohara and Yap, 2018), we speculate that regulation of translational machinery may play an important role in directing the developmental program.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the translation gene expression patterns.

claim: Some bacteria build alternative ribosomes to improve fitness on different growth conditions by altering the core ribosomal protein stoichiometry and differential expression of paralogous ribosomal proteins.
source: It is known that some bacteria build alternative ribosomes to improve fitness on different growth conditions by altering the core ribosomal protein stoichiometry and differential expression of paralogous ribosomal proteins (Foster and Parish, 1973; Nanamiya et al., 2004; Hensley et al., 2012; Prisic et al., 2015; Slavov et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some ribosomal proteins play extraribosomal functions, such as control of transcription or mRNA decay.
source: In addition, some ribosomal proteins also play extraribosomal functions, such as control of transcription or mRNA decay (Warner and McIntosh, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warner and McIntosh, 2009.

claim: 21 one-component system genes were developmentally regulated.
source: 21 OCS genes were developmentally regulated, 9 of which were down-regulated.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DG analysis.

claim: 9 one-component system genes were down-regulated during development.
source: 21 OCS genes were developmentally regulated, 9 of which were down-regulated.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DG analysis.

claim: Of the 272 encoded TCS genes, 47 were included in the developmental groups: 23 HKs, 10 hybrid HKs, and 14 RRs.
source: Of the 272 encoded TCS genes, we found 47 included in the DGs: 23 HKs, 10 hybrid HKs (HyHKs, containing HK and RR modules in the same polypeptide), and 14 RRs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DG analysis.

claim: 6 TCS genes were shut down during development.
source: 6 TCS genes were shut down during development (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Only 16 of 47 TCS genes in the developmental groups have been previously characterized.
source: Only 16 of 47 TCS genes have been previously characterized, thus pinpointing additional candidates for further characterization.
evidence: This is a result from comparing DG genes to characterized genes.

claim: Nine sigma factor genes were found to be developmentally regulated in a sequential fashion.
source: Regarding other transcription factors, nine sigma factor genes were found to be developmentally regulated in a sequential fashion (Figure 10C), including those encoding the major sigma factor RpoD (Inouye, 1990) and RpoN (sigma 54) (Keseler and Kaiser, 1997).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: rpoD was down-regulated at 6 hr, up-regulated during aggregation, and then down-regulated during sporulation.
source: While rpoD was down-regulated at 6 hr, up-regulated during aggregation, and then down-regulated during sporulation, rpoN is up-regulated throughout development (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: rpoN is up-regulated throughout M. xanthus development.
source: While rpoD was down-regulated at 6 hr, up-regulated during aggregation, and then down-regulated during sporulation, rpoN is up-regulated throughout development (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The expression profiles of rpoN and bEBP genes are consistent with previous results demonstrating that a bEBP cascade is triggered upon starvation.
source: The expression profiles of rpoN and bEBP genes are consistent with previous results demonstrating that a bEBP cascade is triggered upon starvation (Giglio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to Giglio et al., 2011.

claim: M. xanthus encodes 99 serine/threonine protein kinases (STPKs), 11 of which are predicted to be pseudokinases.
source: M. xanthus encodes 99 STPKs, 11 of which have been reported to be pseudokinases, because they lack at least one of the three required catalytic residues (Muñoz-Dorado et al., 1991; Pérez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Muñoz-Dorado et al., 1991 and Pérez et al., 2008.

claim: 22 STPK genes were included in the developmental groups.
source: 22 STPK genes were included in the DGs (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Seven STPK genes in the developmental groups encode pseudokinases while 15 encode predicted active kinases.
source: Interestingly, seven encode pseudokinases while 15 encode predicted active kinases (Figure 3—source datas 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a result from the DG analysis.

claim: A high number of regulators directs the developmental program of M. xanthus, with some acting simultaneously and others sequentially.
source: Together, these observations suggest that a high number of regulators directs the developmental program of M. xanthus, with some acting simultaneously and others sequentially to perfectly modulate the different events that occur through development.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression patterns of regulatory genes.

claim: In Caulobacter crescentus, more than 19% of the genes have been found to be developmentally regulated.
source: In other model bacteria such as Caulobacter crescentus, more than 19% of the genes have been found to be developmentally regulated (Laub et al., 2000), a similar percentage to that found in M. xanthus, 57% of which are under direct control of the five master regulators identified in this bacterium (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Laub et al., 2000.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, out of 4100 genes, 520 were dependent on Spo0A, but not on σF, while 66 were dependent upon both regulatory proteins.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, out of 4100 genes, 520 were dependent on Spo0A, but not on σF, while 66 were dependent upon both regulatory proteins (Fawcett et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fawcett et al., 2000.

claim: In Streptomyces coelicolor, 1901 genes (24% of the ORFs) exhibit differences when the substrate mycelium differentiates to a multinucleated mycelium.
source: And in the case of Streptomyces coelicolor, 1901 genes (24% of the ORFs) exhibit differences when the substrate mycelium differentiates to a multinucleated mycelium, with a large number of transcriptional regulators involved (Yagüe et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yagüe et al., 2013.

claim: The developmental mRNA expression profiling will act as a blueprint for the complete elucidation of the M. xanthus developmental regulatory program.
source: Undoubtedly, the developmental mRNA expression profiling presented here will act as a blueprint for the complete elucidation of the M. xanthus developmental regulatory program.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future utility of the data.

claim: The expression profiles of spiA and fmgE from β-galactosidase transcriptional reporters were similar to and in agreement with the RNA-Seq data.
source: Comparison of these β-galactosidase activities to the RNA-Seq data indicated the patterns were similar and in agreement with those obtained with other strategies (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing two different measurement methods shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression profiles of many previously characterized genes from β-galactosidase reporter activity, qRT-PCR, or microarray analyses showed general agreement with the RNA-Seq data.
source: Moreover, the expression profiles of many genes that have been previously characterized from β-galactosidase reporter activity, qRT-PCR, or microarray analyses were compared with those obtained with our data. This analysis revealed a general agreement (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing RNA-Seq data to previous studies.

claim: 142 genes (9.1%) passing quality criteria were not significantly up- or down-regulated during the developmental program and could be considered constitutively expressed.
source: Some of these genes (142; 9.1%) were not significantly (>2 fold) up- or down regulated during the developmental program, suggesting these genes could be considered constitutively expressed.
evidence: This is a result from the expression analysis with an interpretation.

claim: Randomization of the time point RPKM values yielded a false discovery rate of 3.97% based on five randomized simulations.
source: Randomization of the time point RPKM values within each replicate data set yielded a false discovery rate of 3.97% based on five randomized simulations that scrambled the order of the time points across all genes in the two datasets.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the quality control analysis.
